title: The voice of optimization
contribution: Recasts parametric convex and mixed-integer convex optimization as multiclass classification of the optimal 'strategy' (tight constraints plus integer values), learned with optimal classification trees or neural networks after Good-Turing-controlled sampling; on generated LP, QP, MILO and MIQO benchmarks the predicted strategies recover feasible, near-optimal solutions in 89-100% of test cases, with speed-ups over Gurobi ranging from none to several thousand times (arXiv v3 read).
problem_entry: DA+ML+IO: practitioners treat solvers as black boxes and solve many similar instances with varying parameters; goal: predict the optimal solution as parameters vary, interpretably; regressing the solution directly is dismissed as intractable and imprecise (pp. 1-2, 9, 12).
key_idea: Encode the optimum as a strategy (tight constraints; plus integer values for MIO), label sampled parameters with the solver, learn parameter-to-strategy as multiclass classification (OCT, OCT-H, NN), and online solve only the reduced problem of the top 3 predicted strategies, a KKT linear system for LO/QO/MILO/MIQO; stop sampling by a Good-Turing bound on unseen strategies (pp. 2, 10, 14, 17-23).
assumptions: f and g convex in x, any dependence on the parameters; every parameter feasible; i.i.d. samples only; experiments draw parameters from narrow intervals or balls around set points on generated textbook problems (transportation, Markowitz, facility location, hybrid-vehicle MIQO), no real data; relies on few strategies occurring (|S| <= 43 in all tables) (pp. 7-11, 20, 22-31).
proof_devices: Support constraints number at most n (Hoffman 1979; Calafiore 2010), bounding the label space when n << m (p. 9)
Fixing the integer part turns the MIO into a continuous convex problem with the same optimal cost (p. 14)
Theorem 3.1: Good-Turing missing-mass bound N1/N + c sqrt((1/N) ln(3/beta)), c = 2 sqrt 2 + sqrt 3, cited from McAllester-Schapire (2000, Thm 9) (p. 19)

Algorithm 1 stops on the bound, but MLOPT stops when the point estimate is below 0.005; my arithmetic (beta not stated): at N = 10,000 the confidence term alone is about 0.09 for beta = 0.05, so about 3.4 million samples would be needed for epsilon = 0.005 (pp. 20-21, 25-31)
No analysis links classification error to suboptimality; robustness of wrong predictions shown only empirically (pp. 22-31)
experiments: Dell R730 cluster (28 E5-2680 CPUs, 256 GB, K80); Gurobi cited only as the 2020 manual, no version; OCT/OCT-H (OptimalTrees.jl) vs NN (PyTorch) with small tuning grids; N = 10,000 training and 100 test samples; accuracy = feasible and within 1e-3 of optimal; transportation up to 6,400 variables (95-100%, speed-ups at most about 5x, Gurobi faster when small), portfolio up to 400 assets (100%, speed-up not significant), facility location up to 6,480 variables (100%, up to 2,201x), hybrid control T = 10-40 (89-100%, up to 6,846x; at T = 40 OCT 93%, OCT-H 89%, NN 100%); training 2-12 hours; losing rows printed (pp. 20-31).
positioning: Sets itself apart from algorithm configuration (ParamILS, SMAC, irace), learned heuristics (branching, MIQP linearization, decomposition), RL for combinatorial problems, CP/SAT (SATzilla), and learning parametric programs, criticising Misra et al. 2019 directly and Klaucko et al. 2019; distinguishes sensitivity analysis (his LO textbook ch. 5) by deterministic data and MIO reach (pp. 3-6).
writing: Brand metaphor ('give optimization a voice'); headline '90%-100%' and 'significantly faster' while Table 4 has an 89% row and the body reports insignificant speed-ups and solver wins; generated benchmarks called 'realistic examples'; Enigma digression; small shallow-tree examples before benchmarks; self-contained appendices; v3 abstract narrows the claim but the v3 body keeps 'novel, reliable and insightful' and 'any' (pp. 1, 7, 10-19, 24-26, 31-36).
limits_future: Stated: training time, feasibility assumption, OCT accuracy degrades as strategies multiply, no speed gain on small instances or portfolios. Future: online use via the sibling online-MIO paper. Unstated (my reading): narrow parameter balls, no real parameter histories, untested claim to beat (s, S) policies, theorem-implementation gap (pp. 6, 8, 12, 23-26, 32).

method_links.note: Direction reversed: optimization is recast as classification instead of another tradition's problem recast as LP/conic/MIO; the class-keeping move survives online (a known strategy turns an MIO into a smaller convex problem, and LO/QO/MILO/MIQO into a KKT linear system).

For: tuned duel against the strongest learner (NN), stated machine, decision-quality metrics, losing rows printed. Against: no exact or certified tree, solver version unstated; Tension T1 evidence: Appendix A says MIO training runs 'in a reasonable amount of time' (p. 33) but the package trains OCTs by local search with random restarts (p. 34).

Decisions, not labels, are scored (accurate only if the recovered solution is feasible and within 1e-3 of optimal; top 3 strategies tried), but there is no owner, partner data or current rule; the time baseline is the solver. Heuristic 5 (learn the optimizer's strategy offline) is evidenced; its 'narrow the claims' half holds for the v3 abstract only (pp. 1, 7, 32).

Interpretability priced in accuracy (OCT below OCT-H, OCT-H close to NN) with the bad case printed (T = 40) and depth or split sparsity as knobs, but no curve or bound, and the abstract folds the 89% case into '90%-100%' (Tension T6).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The optimum is compressed to a strategy (tight constraints plus integer values) so a parametric optimization problem becomes multiclass classification with a small label set
Sample parameters until the estimated probability of an unseen strategy is small; replaces a four-parameter sampling scheme of prior work

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: explain the optimizer with an interpretable model
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Optimal trees read as policies over parameters (inventory: wait t0 periods, then order the demand; knapsack and supplier rules), so that trees 'give optimization a voice'

transferable: Encode each parametric optimum as (tight-constraint set, integer values) and learn it as a class label; online, solve only the reduced problem, which for LO/QO/MILO/MIQO is a KKT linear system with no solver at run time (pp. 10, 14, 21).

Sample parameters in batches until the Good-Turing estimate N1/N of unseen strategies is small; if you claim the high-confidence bound, compute the N it requires, since the point estimate is all the implementation controls (pp. 19-21).

Score a learned optimizer by its decisions: normalized violation and relative suboptimality with explicit tolerances, maximum over test points; let it propose top-k strategies and keep the best after solving each reduced problem (pp. 22-23).
Report the speed ratio against the solver for every size, keeping rows where the solver wins (pp. 24-26).
Show the mechanism on small instances with shallow trees whose leaves read as policies, then move to large benchmarks (pp. 10-12).

quotes.text: Instead, our approach encodes the optimal solution with a small amount of information that we denote as strategy.
OCTs show competitive accuracy in most comparisons apart from the cases with higher number of strategies where the prediction performance degrades.

title: A unified approach to mixed-integer optimization problems with logical constraints
contribution: Reads big-M as one of two regularizers (big-M or ridge) for on/off logical constraints, dualizes the inner continuous problem into a mixed-integer saddle-point problem convex in the binaries, and solves it by single-tree outer approximation with Boolean-relaxation bounds, rounding and local search; this unifies big-M, perspective and ridge formulations and beats CPLEX's direct formulations on several large classes, with gaps and losing cases reported (arXiv v3 read).
problem_entry: IO+ML (CP devices; AP testbeds): a modelling convention, big-M since Glover 1975, which textbooks present as part of the problem although it reformulates logical constraints; the abstract says 'we challenge this longstanding modeling practice'; problem (1.1) covers network design, sparse ERM, sparse portfolio, unit commitment, facility location, sparse PCA, BQP and unions of ellipsoids (pp. 1-7).
key_idea: Substitute v = Diag(z)x, regularize with big-M or ridge, dualize: f(z) = max h(alpha) - sum z_i Omega*(alpha_i) is convex in z with subgradients from one continuous solve on supp(z); run outer approximation in one branch-and-bound via lazy callbacks; Boolean relaxation for bounds and root cuts; rounding and local search for incumbents; ridge removes cut degeneracy and recovers perspective cuts (pp. 8-16).
assumptions: Omega is the big-M indicator or ridge (decomposable, convex, minimized at 0); each inner problem infeasible or strongly dual; conic feasibility cuts assume conic g ('some loss of generality'); rounding bound needs a uniform bound L on |alpha*|; admitted: big-M infeasible below M0, ridge changes the objective for any gamma; data: synthetic network design and ERM, Biq-Mac BQP, six PCA sets, Wilshire 5000 and Russell 1000, 112 OR-Library facility instances, Frangioni-Gentile unit commitment (pp. 7-12, 14, 17-23, 27-28).
proof_devices: Nonlinear reformulation v = Diag(z)x plus Fenchel duality on the coupling constraint; z_i^2 = z_i linearizes the ridge term (Theorem 2.5, p. 9)
Remark 2.6: regularization as a relaxation replacing hard dual constraints alpha_i = 0 if z_i = 1 by a soft penalty (p. 9)
Convexity of f as a pointwise maximum of linear functions; outer-approximation cut (2.16); ridge gives strong concavity, hence unique alpha* and no degeneracy (p. 10)
Proposition 2.9: Lipschitz-type bounds with constants proportional to M or gamma (pp. 10-11)

Theorem 3.1: randomized rounding of the Boolean relaxation is epsilon-optimal with probability at least 1 - |R| exp(-epsilon^2/kappa); proof by a sub-Gaussian maximum over the l1 ball's extreme points; my reading: the gap bound grows like M L |R| sqrt(ln|R|) (pp. 14-15, 26)
Theorem 3.2: ridge dual gives the perspective formulation; perspective cuts are the outer-approximation cuts (p. 16; proof p. 27)
Coercive regularizer rules out asymptotic feasibility, so conic infeasibility certificates exist (footnote 5, p. 13)
Lemma B.1 and Corollary B.2: explicit L under strong concavity (pp. 27-28)
Printed boundaries: exponential worst case of outer approximation (p. 12); two-moment SDP relaxations usually intractable for n > 300 (p. 15)
experiments: Julia 1.0, JuMP 0.18.4, CPLEX 12.8.0, one Xeon core, 32 GB; opponent: CPLEX on big-M or MISOCP. Network design m = 40-200, 1 h: big-M cuts better in 94% of 100 instances (9.9% average, up to 40%), ridge cuts 11% better than MISOCP, gaps mostly > 100%. BQP: Goemans-Williamson warm start, only bqp-50/100 solved; the 'faster than CPLEX' claim holds only with triangle inequalities (my reading of Table 4); better incumbents everywhere; only the cuts fit 32 GB on bqp-1000. ERM, PCA, portfolio summarized from companion papers (100,000s of features; 3,200 vs 400 securities). Facility location (112 instances): cuts faster in only 12.7% (big-M) and 23.85% (ridge) of instances; ablation table, whose ridge row does not match the text. Unit commitment: big-M faster for alpha <= 1, ridge MISOCP for alpha >= 2 (pp. 17-23, 29).
positioning: Joins two literatures 'often considered in isolation': forcing-constraint formulations (Glover big-M, Bienstock, perspective cuts, MISOCP, ridge) and decomposition (Benders, generalized Benders, outer approximation, branch-and-cut, modern Benders, Pareto cuts); claims a new general link to perspective cuts; heavy self-citation (six of 55 references; three experiment subsections from companion papers) (pp. 2-3, 13, 16, 19-21, 24-26).
writing: Abstract: class, convention, 'we challenge this longstanding modeling practice', reformulation, headline numbers (Heuristic 9 skeleton); 'Duality to the Rescue'; merits summaries from theoretical, algorithmic and experimental angles with explicit routing advice; hedges on untested points ('we intuit', 'This suggests', 'We believe'); numbered practical guidelines (pp. 1, 8-9, 11, 13-14, 16-17, 23-24).
limits_future: Regularizer choice instance-dependent; efficiency hinges on fast separation and cardinality structure; ridge changes the objective; big-M can make the problem infeasible; no restarts or multi-threading; uninformative gaps on network design; no code link in the arXiv text. Future: other regularizers, higher-level relaxations, mixed-integer semidefinite optimization (pp. 9, 11, 13, 15, 17-18, 21-24).

method_links.note: The model (the regularizer) is redesigned so a standard solver's lazy callbacks apply; the dual is read for cuts and uniqueness; boundaries are printed. Bears on Method 1's limitation and Tension T4: by 2019-2021 the group named big-M's instability and weak bounds and preferred ridge or perspective formulations when the objective is strongly convex; not a reply to the OCT big-M critique and silent on trees, so the Roundtable Card's blind spot 'formulation strength' should be narrowed, not dropped.

Warm starts (Boolean relaxation, rounding, local search; Goemans-Williamson for BQP), exact branch-and-cut under a stated limit with solver version and machine, gaps printed even above 100%, duel against the solver's own formulation, an ablation, and losing cases printed.

One knob (M or gamma), a solution-independent rounding bound that 'quantifies the price of fixing variables', and published curves with the bad case (M < 1/k infeasible); but the priced property is tractability, not a property a decision-maker wants.

Reopening driven by remodelling, not a rebuilt solver-times-hardware figure; the 'why now' is qualitative (solver improvements; lazy callbacks 'now standard tools'); the only numbers are scale ratios against previous attempts, including three orders of magnitude over his own 2016 big-M best-subset paper.
Umbrella paper over two students' lines (Cory-Wright, Pauphilet); three experiment subsections are drawn from companion papers [8], [9], [12].

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: re-read a modelling convention as a hidden, tunable modelling choice
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Big-M recast as a regularizer, with ridge as an alternative chosen by tractability, not habit
Ridge makes the inner dual strongly concave so outer-approximation cuts are unique, recommended instead of Pareto-optimal cut selection
Theoretical (Table 2), algorithmic (section 3.5) and experimental (section 4.4) summaries route the reader to big-M or ridge

transferable: For on/off logical constraints, write x_i = 0 if z_i = 0 as v = Diag(z)x, add a decomposable convex regularizer minimized at 0 (big-M box or ridge) and dualize the inner problem: f(z) = max h(alpha) - sum z_i Omega*(alpha_i) is convex in z and one continuous solve on supp(z) gives the cut (pp. 8-10, 13).
Run outer approximation as one branch-and-bound with lazy callbacks, cutting at binary (sparse) z; for infeasible subproblems add the no-good cut or a conic infeasibility-certificate cut (pp. 12-13).

Feed the root: Boolean relaxation (Kelley or dual subgradient ascent) for a lower bound and initial cuts; Bernoulli rounding and subgradient-guided sequential rounding; one-flip local search that stops on cycling (pp. 14-16).
Derive natural regularizers from data: M from flow conservation, 1/gamma = lambda_min(Q), or a diagonal q from max e'q s.t. Q - Diag(q) PSD (p. 8).
Compare formulations that optimize different objectives by re-evaluating each returned z at the unregularized cost, not by gaps (pp. 17-18).
Choose big-M vs ridge by scaling the objective's quadratic coefficient and timing both formulations (p. 22).
Ablate the recipe on a public library (OA + lower-bound step, OA + upper-bound step, OA + both) and report the share of wins and mean improvement (pp. 21-22).

quotes.text: In this work, we challenge this longstanding modeling practice and express the logical constraints in a non-linear way.
We argue that regularization is a modeling choice that impacts the tractability of the formulation and should be made accordingly.

title: Integrated multimodal artificial intelligence framework for healthcare applications
contribution: A modular multimodal pipeline (HAIM) that turns MIMIC-IV patient records (tabular data, time series, notes, X-rays) into one fusion embedding from frozen pre-trained extractors and trains XGBoost on every subset of 11 sources (14,324 models), reporting AUROC gains of 6-33% over the average single-source model and Shapley-measured modality value across 12 prediction tasks; predictions only; directed, not written, by Bertsimas (published version read).
problem_entry: AP+ML (no optimization model): multimodal clinical AI is promising but unified, scalable pipelines that beat single-modality systems remain hard to build, and prior work assumes multimodality helps without validating how performance changes as modalities are added (pp. 1, 4).
key_idea: Patient-centric files; one embedding per source from frozen, exchangeable extractors (tabular normalization, time-series statistics, Clinical BERT with 512-token chunk averaging, DenseNet121-res224-chex probabilities and dense features); concatenation into a 4,845-dimensional vector; XGBoost on every non-empty subset of sources; Shapley attribution of AUROC to sources and modalities (pp. 3, 6-8).
assumptions: MIMIC-IV v1.0 plus MIMIC-CXR-JPG v2.0.0 restricted to patients with a chest X-ray (34,537 samples, 7,279 stays, 6,485 patients); labels from radiology-note annotations (confirmed only), 48 h discharge and 48 h mortality; radiology notes excluded as inputs for chest tasks; a single learner (XGBoost) chosen heuristically; Shapley with AUROC 0.5 for no source; missing-data handling only in the supplement (not read); MIMIC only exemplifies the pipeline (pp. 1, 3, 6-8).
proof_devices: n/a: no optimization formulation, algorithm analysis or proof (pp. 1-10)
Exhaustive enumeration of all non-empty source subsets: 2,047 per task with 11 sources, 1,023 per chest task with 10 (p. 8)
Shapley values over 11 sources and 4 modalities on test AUROC, empty set 0.5, modality AUROC = average over its sources' models; small or negative values read as information loss (p. 3)
experiments: 14,324 XGBoost models, each on five patient-stratified 80/20 splits with fivefold CV grid search inside training (depth 5-8, 200 or 300 trees, learning rate 0.05/0.1/0.3); metric: mean and SD of test AUROC; gains measured against the average single-source model (chest 6-22%, length of stay 8-20%, mortality 11-33%); images dominate chest tasks, time series dominate the others; diminishing returns; MIT Supercloud, one V100 per instance; no external validation, calibration or clinical-score comparator. My checks: 11-source per-modality counts sum to 2,046, not 2,047; Evd/Evmp dimensions swapped in the list; N = 45,050 exceeds the 34,537 samples (pp. 1, 3-4, 7-8).
positioning: Among single-specialty multimodal systems and a 2020 review; 'Qualitatively' improves on Li et al.; three stated differences: systematic combinatorial study of adding modalities, modular open-source extractors instead of ad-hoc fused architectures, many sources and modalities with Shapley values; no optimization or OR citations; one self-citation (pp. 1-5, 9).
writing: Nature-family layout; abstract from AI's promise to scale numbers to the headline 'by 6–33%'; 'To our knowledge' novelty; dense hedging ('appears', 'suggest', 'could potentially'); lettered contributions (A)-(C); contributions statement assigns writing to four first authors and direction and editing to Bertsimas (pp. 1-6, 9).
limits_future: Stated: MIMIC only exemplifies the pipeline, only XGBoost tested, diminishing returns and redundancy, negative Shapley values as error propagation. Future: other extractors, deployment in clinical and operational settings, more holistic data. Unstated (my reading): single-centre data, no decision analysis, average-model baseline (pp. 1, 3-6).

method_links.note: Predictions only: no decision scored, no owner's rule as baseline (APACHE named, not compared), and the headline gain is measured against the average single-source model rather than the strongest, the opposite of step 2's 'prefer the stronger naive rule'; SKILL.md warning sign 4 applies.

The final learner is greedy boosted trees chosen heuristically from seven architectures that exclude his optimal trees; no exact model or certificate. Scope caveat: the paper's question is data integration, not the learner.

Cohort-scale programme work: six equal-contribution first authors, four of whom planned and wrote while eight authors coded and analyzed and he directed and edited; open-source code and a reusable data asset on PhysioNet (Heuristic 6: build the data asset); Jameel Clinic funding.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: value data sources by exhaustive subset training plus Shapley attribution
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: A model for every non-empty subset of 11 sources (14,324 in total) and Shapley values over sources and modalities on test AUROC

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: frozen modular extractors producing one patient vector reused across tasks
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Exchangeable pre-trained extractors per modality, concatenated into a fixed 4,845-dimensional embedding used for 12 tasks; an extractor can be swapped without retraining the others

transferable: To value data sources, train one model per non-empty subset of sources (2^k - 1), repeat over patient-stratified splits, and compute Shapley values of sources and modalities on test AUROC with 0.5 for the empty set (pp. 3, 8).
Keep each test split unseen at the level of every model: tune by k-fold CV inside the training split only, stratify splits by patient (pp. 7-8).
Drop any input from which the label was derived, e.g. radiology notes when labels come from radiology notes (pp. 7-8).
For notes longer than the encoder's 512-token window, embed each chunk and average; for several images per patient, average per-image probability and dense-feature embeddings (p. 7).
coauthors: Luis R. Soenksen, Yu Ma, Cynthia Zeng, Leonard Boussioux, Kimberly Villalobos Carballo, Liangyuan Na, Holly M. Wiberg, Michael L. Li, Ignacio Fuentes

quotes.text: Previous works in this field assume advantageous properties to multimodality without clear validation of the dynamics of such expected performance benefits as data modalities are added.
D.B. directed overall research and edited the paper.
